Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette:
Tane was a 39-year-old airline pilot of Oceanian background who had come to treatment after years of trying to keep functioning as if nothing had happened. He described himself as someone who had always valued composure, routine, and precision, and for a long time he had pushed himself to keep those qualities intact after the night he was stopped by police. The incident had occurred years earlier, on an ordinary evening after he had been out with a friend. He was driving home when he was pulled over, and what began as a routine stop escalated into a frightening confrontation in which officers closed in on him physically and treated him as though he were dangerous. Tane spoke about the crush of bodies in close proximity, the sense that there was nowhere to step back, and the raw nausea he felt in his stomach as the situation intensified. Even now, he said that remembering the scene did not feel like recalling something that was over; it felt as if the same terror returned in full, with his body reacting before he had time to think. When he tried to tell the story, he often shook his head and said it still seemed unreal, "too extreme" to have happened to him, yet at the same time the details came back with a vividness that ordinary memories never had. He would describe the lights, the voices, and the tightness around him as though he were there again, and he was certain that the memory was more real than the ordinary events of his day-to-day life.

In the months that followed, Tane began to notice that certain situations no longer felt neutral. Being physically close to unfamiliar people made him tense immediately, and he found himself measuring distance in a way he had not before. In ordinary public settings, if a stranger approached him directly, he felt threatened before anything was said. He described scanning faces and shoulders automatically, bracing for contact or confrontation. The same sense of alarm appeared when he was in traffic with other people in the car. Driving with others, even when the trip was simple, became uncomfortable because he felt trapped beside them and unable to control how close they were. He also became increasingly aware of nausea in his body, and this sensation itself began to unsettle him; when he felt nauseous, he would pull his attention inward, wondering whether something was happening again and whether he would lose control in front of others.

At work, these reactions showed up in subtle but important ways. As an airline pilot, Tane spent his days in controlled, highly structured environments, yet even there he found himself reacting to things that others seemed to ignore. When a process took longer than expected, such as a delay in turnaround, a pause in coordination, or waiting for someone else to respond, he was quickly on edge and would assume something bad was happening. He disliked not knowing what was going on and felt compelled to stay alert to every change in timing. Ordinary sounds also affected him; a sudden clatter, a sharp call, or an unexpected bang could make him jump in a way that embarrassed him. He said that he knew most people would not react so strongly, which made the response feel even more unsettling. Over time he tried to manage by keeping himself busy and avoiding situations that made him feel too exposed, but this narrowed the way he moved through daily life. He became more guarded around strangers, less comfortable being in close quarters, and increasingly careful about arrangements that involved riding with other people.

Tane's divorce had taken place after these changes had already become established, and he spoke about the strain of trying to explain to others why he seemed so watchful and uneasy. He had not initially sought help because he believed he should be able to handle it himself, but after realizing that the terror of the memory still flooded him whenever he recalled the stop, and after seeing how often he was reacting to delays, proximity, strangers, and ordinary sounds, he finally agreed to come in. What brought him to treatment was the sense that he could no longer keep pretending the event belonged in the past. More than anything, he said he wanted to stop feeling as though danger could appear at any moment when someone came too close, when a routine changed, or when his body signaled nausea. He was afraid that if he did nothing, he would keep shrinking his world, yet he was also hoping that with help he might reclaim enough steadiness to move through life and work without constantly bracing for the next threat.
